title: Large Language Model-Guided Discovery of Weight-Five Bivariate Bicycle Codes
abstract: Building on our earlier program-evolution workflow guided by large language models (LLMs), we study weight-five bivariate bicycle (BB) and perturbed bivariate bicycle (PBB) codes. The resulting catalogue contains 1,142 distinct code proposals, including 1,081 nonbaseline proposals attributable to LLM-generated programs. Across the catalogue, we certify connected Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) realizations [[96,4,10]], [[140,6,10]], and [[180,4,14]]. A post-search comparison certifies seven imported Lin--Pryadko archive constructions. For leading parameter triples also represented in that archive, we provide exact distance evidence, explicit bivariate presentations, and verified component reductions. A basis-independent connectivity analysis identifies 409 of the 1,142 catalogue entries as disconnected and shows that 73.1\% of the classes with exact distance certificates contain repeated connected components. Algebraic analysis organizes the connected CSS classes into order-3, order-7, and order-15 cyclotomic-kernel strata. The strongest exact connected PBB parameter point is [[216,4,10]], attained by two distinct component classes. Among the 936 distinct CSS proposals from the LLM-guided campaign with a recorded positive distance, 816 (87.18\%) are certified at $d\geq5$. For comparison, three random-search controls each sample 6,444 CSS code proposals uniformly without replacement, using the same per-lattice and encoded-dimension sample counts as the LLM-guided campaign. In these controls, 4,672--4,785 proposals (72.50--74.26\%) meet the same criterion. The LLM-guided campaign has the higher certified yield, while the random controls cover more connected classes. Together, these results extend LLM-guided discovery to a more constrained code family and provide a reproducible structural and exact-distance account of its strongest candidates.
summary: This work details the discovery and rigorous characterization of specific quantum error-correcting codes (BB and PBB) using a novel search protocol guided by Large Language Models. The LLM-guided search successfully generated a large catalogue of code proposals, achieving a high certified yield of codes with large minimum distances. This advances the field by providing a reproducible, AI-assisted structural account of these complex quantum codes.
main_problem: The paper focuses on the discovery and detailed characterization of weight-five bivariate bicycle (BB) and perturbed bivariate bicycle (PBB) quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes.
main_result: The LLM-guided search generated a large catalogue of code proposals, with a high percentage (87.18%) of the generated CSS proposals certified to have a distance $d \ge 5$.
method: The research employs a novel program-evolution workflow guided by Large Language Models (LLMs) to systematically search for and certify quantum error-correcting codes.
model_or_system: The system under study is a set of quantum error-correcting codes, specifically CSS and PBB codes, which are analyzed using their stabilizer generators and associated parameters $(k, d, n)$.
key_observables: Code parameters $(k, d, n)$, connectivity (connected vs. disconnected components), and the Figure of Merit (FOM) = $k d^2 / n$.
important_parameters: Weight-five stabilizer generators, block lengths $72 \le n \le 432$, and the specific code type (BB/PBB).
main_assumptions: The comparison with random controls and established literature constructions (Lin–Pryadko archive) is used to validate the LLM-guided search results.
figures_summary: The notes do not describe specific figures, but mention tables summarizing certification outcomes and structural analysis.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of defining the problem (BB/PBB codes), detailing the LLM-guided search methodology, presenting the resulting catalogue size and certification statistics, and concluding with structural and algebraic organization of the best candidates.
why_interesting: The integration of LLMs into the discovery process for highly structured mathematical objects like quantum codes represents a significant methodological advance for theoretical quantum information scientists.
